name: Bumchu at Tashiding
when: February or March (14th and 15th days of the first Tibetan month)
summary: Bumchu is a two-day festival at Tashiding Monastery, 19 km from Yuksom, when lamas open a sealed vase of sacred water and read its level as a forecast for Sikkim's year. Pilgrims come from Sikkim, Nepal, Bhutan and Darjeeling to receive a few drops.
body: The name means 'sacred vase'. According to tradition the vase was blessed in the eighteenth century and is kept sealed at Tashiding all year. On the night of the 14th day of the first month of the Tibetan calendar, the lamas open it in front of the assembled crowd. If the water stands at the brim, the year will bring peace and plenty; if it spills over, disaster or unrest; if it is low or nearly dry, famine.

Some of the water is then poured out for pilgrims, the vase is topped up from the Rathong Chu and sealed again for the next year. Thousands of people camp on and around the hill, and the courtyards fill with prayer, butter lamps and stalls selling food and offerings.
Tashiding itself is one of the most sacred sites in Sikkim, a conical hill covered in chortens between the Rathong and Rangeet rivers. Bumchu is the time when it is busiest and most alive.
tips: Book a room in Yuksom, Tashiding or Pelling well ahead; rooms near the monastery fill weeks before.
Expect the main ritual late at night and into the early morning; dress for cold.
Arrive at the hill by afternoon to find a place, and keep a torch handy for the steep path.
Follow the crowd's lead on where to stand; never push towards the vase or the lamas.
Check the exact dates each year; they follow the Tibetan lunar calendar.

faqs.a: Bumchu falls on the 14th and 15th days of the first month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, which usually lands in February or March. The dates move every year, so check the Sikkim government holiday list or ask Tashiding Monastery a few months ahead. Check current status before you travel, as crowd rules may change.

At Tashiding Monastery in West Sikkim, on a hilltop about 19 km from Yuksom and 40 km from Pelling. From the road head a steep path climbs to the monastery in 20–30 minutes. There is limited parking during the festival, so expect to walk further than usual and to queue.

Yes. Visitors are welcome to watch and to receive the blessed water. Dress modestly, keep a respectful distance from the ritual, and ask before photographing monks or pilgrims. Crowds are large and the hill is steep, so it is not ideal for small children or anyone unsteady on their feet.

faqs.q: What happens to the sacred water
faqs.a: The lamas pour some of the water from the vase into smaller containers and share it among pilgrims, who take a few drops as a blessing or carry it home for family. The vase is then refilled with water from the Rathong Chu and sealed again until the next Bumchu.

name: Pang Lhabsol at Ravangla
when: Late August or September (15th day of the seventh Tibetan month)
summary: Pang Lhabsol honours Mount Kangchenjunga as Sikkim's guardian deity and remembers a blood-brotherhood pact between the Lepcha and Bhutia peoples. Ravangla holds one of the biggest public celebrations, with masked warrior dances, cultural shows and a fair.
body: The festival is unique to Sikkim. It was given its present form by the third Chogyal, Chakdor Namgyal, in the early eighteenth century. At its heart are the masked dances, in which monks dressed as Dzonga, the deity of Kangchenjunga, and his attendant Mahakala perform with warriors in old battle dress.

Ravangla has become a focus for the celebrations, with a cultural festival and fair held over several days alongside the monastic rituals. Ralang Monastery nearby also marks the day. In Gangtok the main dances take place at the Tsuklakhang palace monastery.
Because it falls at the tail of the monsoon, rain is likely and roads can be slow. The reward is a festival that is still mostly local.
tips: Carry an umbrella and rain jacket; late August and September are still wet.
Book Ravangla rooms early, as the town is small and fills for the festival.
Allow extra travel time for monsoon landslides on the roads from Gangtok and Siliguri.
Watch the masked dances from the edge of the ground and never cross the dance area.
Check the year's dates and programme locally; they follow the Tibetan calendar.

faqs.a: It honours Mount Kangchenjunga as the guardian deity of Sikkim and marks a historic oath of brotherhood between the Lepcha and Bhutia peoples, sworn by Lepcha chief Thekong Tek and Bhutia leader Khye Bumsa at Kabi Lungchok. Monks perform masked warrior dances to honour the mountain and its protectors.

It falls on the 15th day of the seventh month of the Tibetan calendar, usually in late August or September. It is a state holiday in Sikkim. Ravangla's celebrations often run over several days around that date. Dates change each year, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Pang Lhabsol at Ravangla or Gangtok better
faqs.a: Gangtok has the classic monastic dances at Tsuklakhang, with tight crowds and limited space. Ravangla has a broader festival with dances, cultural programmes and a fair in a smaller town, and is easier to combine with Buddha Park and Ralang. If you are touring South and West Sikkim, Ravangla makes more sense.

Generally yes, from the spectator areas, without flash. Some moments of the ritual may be off limits for photography, and organisers or monks will say so. Never step into the dance ground for a photo. Drones are usually not allowed. Respect the festival as a religious event first.

name: Tendong Lho Rum Faat
summary: Tendong Lho Rum Faat is the Lepcha festival of thanks to Tendong Hill, which in Lepcha tradition saved the people from a great flood. It is held on 8 August, a state holiday in Sikkim, with prayers, songs and offerings at Tendong and in towns such as Namchi.
body: The Lepchas, Sikkim's earliest known inhabitants, tell that the Teesta and Rangeet once flooded the land and that Tendong Hill rose to keep a group of people above the water. The festival thanks the hill and asks for protection from natural disasters.

Prayers are led by Lepcha priests, known as bongthing and mun. Communities gather in traditional dress for rituals, offerings, songs, dances and cultural programmes. Some groups climb Tendong Hill above Namchi for prayers near the top; others celebrate in Namchi, Gangtok, Kalimpong and Darjeeling.
It is a community festival rather than a tourist show, and a good chance to see Lepcha dress, music and food.
tips: Ask a local contact or your hotel where public programmes are held that year.
Expect monsoon rain and slippery trails if you climb Tendong Hill.
Dress respectfully and ask before photographing elders and priests.
Try Lepcha foods if stalls are set up; ask what each dish is.

faqs.q: When is Tendong Lho Rum Faat
faqs.a: It is held every year on 8 August, a fixed date in the Gregorian calendar, and is a public holiday in Sikkim. Some community programmes may start the day before or continue the day after. Check current status before you travel if you plan to attend a specific event or climb Tendong Hill.

faqs.q: Where can I see Tendong Lho Rum Faat
faqs.a: Prayers are held on Tendong Hill above Namchi and Damthang, and Lepcha associations hold programmes in Namchi, Gangtok, Kalimpong and Darjeeling. Ask your hotel or a local Lepcha association where public events are planned. In Namchi, events are often in or near the town centre.

faqs.q: Can tourists join the Tendong prayers
faqs.a: Visitors are usually welcome to watch public prayers and cultural programmes if they are respectful. Do not interrupt rituals, keep clear of priests and offerings, and ask before taking photos. The climb on Tendong Hill in August is wet and slippery, so go only if you are prepared.

The Lepchas, who call themselves Rongkup or Mutanchi Rongkup, are the earliest known people of Sikkim and the hills around Darjeeling and Kalimpong. They have their own language and script, and traditions rooted in nature worship alongside Buddhism and Christianity. Dzongu in North Sikkim is a protected Lepcha reserve.
